blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Witness statement of DR SALLY OGDEN (read)
As your Lordship knows, this morning the jury will hear evidence that attaches to the counts per training to both [Baby C] and [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: May I begin, with agreement, by reading a statement from Dr Sally Ogden that relates to the case of [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: To assist the injury's understanding of the evidence, can I invite them to open up the [Baby C] sequence of events on their iPads and ask Mr Murphy to put it on our screen at tile 77, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. You will see at tile 77, members of the jury, that we have clinical notes to which Dr Sally Ogden and Dr Gibbs contributed at around 9.30 in the morning of Saturday, 13 June.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we can click behind the tile and go to the original document, the second page, which will -- thank you. Scroll down, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: You may recall Dr Ogden taking us through various notes in relation to -- thank you, Mr Murphy, that's perfect -- her examination of [Baby C] that morning.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This additional statement from Dr Ogden will focus your attention on the last entry at the bottom of the screen that Mr Murphy has projected up for us. The words:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Bowel sounds heard."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Ogden's statement is dated 3 November 2022. She says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "This exhibit [that's the exhibit on the screen] details my physical examination of [Baby C] at 09.30 hours on 13 June 2015. I have previously provided a statement dated 7 November 2018 where I have documented my physical examination findings.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Within my notes I have detailed 'bowel sounds heard' during examination. I can provide the following additional information.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I auscultated [Baby C]'s abdomen for the purpose of listening for bowel sounds as a routine step as part of an examination. As a result, I have documented that bowel sounds were heard, which can be a normal finding on examination and suggests there is some movement within the bowel.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Listening for bowel sounds is part of a detailed checklist of what I see, feel and hear; the normal steps taken during the physical examination of a patient.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Each individual finding is combined to assist with me forming an opinion and would not be taken in isolation.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I can't recall any further details about the bowel sounds and I have not described them in any more detail.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: However, if they had sounded abnormal then I would have documented 'abnormal sounds', which is an important finding when present. It is good practice to document all examination findings, both for the medical records and so future doctors can make any necessary comparison for ongoing care. By reading the notes in their entirety, that examination would detail that the patient's abdominal examination at that time was normal."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That concludes the evidence relating to [Baby C] in that regard.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just as a word of explanation first I'm now going to recall Professor Arthurs, the radiologist. What we are going to do is to deal both with the cases of [Baby C] and with the case of [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I will examine Dr Arthurs on both cases and then Mr Myers will cross-examine on both.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: PROFESSOR OWEN ARTHURS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Welcome back, Professor Arthurs. Just for the sake of the record would you identify yourself again, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I'm Owen Arthurs, I am a consultant radiologist and a professor of radiology at Great Ormond Street Hospital in London.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. Could we today, please, deal individually first with the case of [Baby C] and then, subsequently, the case of [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as [Baby C]'s case is concerned, did you complete a report dated 19 May 2020?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And did you subsequently complete a report that simply referred to or set out material that you had received?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: But in which you didn't supply any further opinion?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Did you then, together with a radiologist instructed on behalf of the defence, a Dr Katharine Halliday, sign a further report in which you gave further opinion relating to each of these two cases?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What I'd like to do, please, is deal with [Baby C] first, then. Did you note in your report [Baby C]'s identity, the date of his birth, his gestation and birth weight and the date of his death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Did you set out in your report the radiographs, the Xray pictures, that you had received and reviewed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'd like to take you through those pictures, please, which we have in a bespoke file on the system, my Lord. There is a total of seven or eight pictures -- I think seven in this file, aren't there, Dr Arthurs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The first is a radiograph taken of [Baby C]'s chest and abdomen on 10 June at 18.19 hours; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, and this is the one that I currently have on the screen.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Perfect, thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just to help us, please, could you point out a few things for us so that the jury can understand? We have heard, and we will hear some more evidence about the diaphragm. Is the diaphragm visible on this picture?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. From the X-ray you can infer where the diaphragm would be. So to begin with, this is a small baby, they fit almost entirely on one size of radiograph that would be standard size. So you have from the neck and then the shoulders, you have the chest, all of the abdomen, even down to the femurs, which you can see on the bottom of the screen. In the top part you will see the heart as being the large blob in the middle, effectively the white blob in the middle, and either side of that are lungs. The reason that lungs appear black on an X-ray is because X-rays pass through them, therefore they contain air.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So immediately below, where the black part ends and the two lung ends, is the diaphragm. It's an anatomical structure that distinguishes the chest from the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Below the diaphragm you can see normal gas in the stomach on the patient's left, the right of our screen, and then normal gas in the small bowel.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Those are the dark areas?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The black areas, that's right, is gas, effectively.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The bowel looks, in some ways, a bit like a string of sausages, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's effectively what it is. It's one long tube from the oesophagus into the stomach, through the small bowel, the large bowel, down to the anus.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So far as that picture is concerned, is there any abnormality?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, I don't think so. The heart looks normal, the lungs are clear. There is normal gas in the stomach and the small bowel. The reason this X-ray is likely to be taken is to check the position of the some of the lines inserted by the medical team and there's an umbilical venous catheter, the UVC, which is the big thick white tube you can see coming in from the bottom and going upwards. The only comment really that would be made on this radiograph is that the tube is in slightly too far and should be brought back down a little.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So just so the jury have the complete picture, that tube appears almost to be overlaid on top of [Baby C] there, but does it pass within his body at some point and, if so, can you point out the approximate location at which it passes in?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The problem with X-rays is that they are twodimensional pictures of what is clearly a three-dimensional structure. So the bottom of the line, as it comes into the radiograph, is clearly outside the patient and at some point it clearly goes inside the patient through the umbilicus, and you can imagine where the belly button would be. And then it passes inside the patient up towards the heart. So I can't point out exactly on that where the belly button is.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: No, right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry. So that I've understood this, I am probably being a bit slow, in other words, because it's in two dimensions, it shouldn't be thought that it's coming in from that direction, it may be coming in outside the body in that direction, but in through the belly button --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: -- in the normal belly button place, in the middle?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's right, in the normal belly button place, allowing for the fact that the baby at this point doesn't have a belly button, but has an umbilical cord, so there's an extent of cord and the catheter will pass into the cord.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: This is the difficulty with interpreting a picture without the baby in front of you because, of course, the medical staff at this point will have known they'll have placed a catheter into the umbilicus, they will know where they expect it to be, and the X-ray is done to check where the position of the tip will be, not where it would be outside the patient.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. So that was the first picture you reviewed?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The second was taken -- so that's taken at 18.19 as we can see. The second, the same day, but at 22.38; is that right? Can we move down to the --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, yes. So this X-ray, taken a few hours later, shows the same baby in the same position with the same lines and things in. You can see that big tube going into the middle of the patient has been withdrawn slightly so we presume -- that was done by the medical team in the interim.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: There's normal gas in the stomach, there's a nasogastric tube in here, and there's normal gas in the small bowel as we saw on the previous radiograph.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So the most striking abnormality on this image is the right-hand lung of the patient, so the patient's left is the right of our image, is white.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What does that denote?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And because you can see the airways as black, you can see the pattern of airways as they go out, it means there's something in the lung stopping the X-rays passing through. The most likely cause for that is infection and that goes by several different words and names that we use. We use opacification to mean whiteness, we use consolidation to mean -- and infection and pneumonia. They're almost interchangeable at that stage.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: When you say that on [Baby C]'s left lung, but the right one as we look at the picture --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: -- you can see the airways, are they the slightly darker -- it almost looks like a scribble or a starburst or something like that within the whiteness.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And this reflects -- if you breathe in, you'll have air in your airway and then into the trachea and the bronchi, but it won't get into an infected lung. So the lung looks white and the airways look black.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: By contrast do we have the right lung, which is to the left of the photograph --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: -- which is almost like a negative of the left one?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's black, as you would expect, with a normal amount of air or gas going into it. So in layman's terms, this child has a left-sided lung infection.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Thank you. The third radiograph is taken on 12 June at 12.36; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right, the 12th, 12.36.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: This is one that the jury has seen already. What abnormality, if any, do we see on that radiograph?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is centred on [Baby C]'s abdomen. Again the diaphragm is at the top and you can see the femurs and the legs at the bottom. There is a tube that crosses the whole of the radiograph, which is oxygen tubing, which is outside of the patient. But the most striking thing about this is there's dilatation of the stomach, so the big gas bubble that you can see at the top of the picture is [Baby C]'s stomach, which is full of gas. The tubes below are then the small and large bowel with gas within them.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just so we can test our own abilities now, at the top left of the picture as we look at it, directly under the 6 for June, so 12/06, where we see that area of blackness at the top of the radiograph, is that the bottom of the right lung?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So the border between that area of blackness and where it starts to go white, is that where the diaphragm is?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, that's the bottom of the right lung.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Implicitly the diaphragm is there because the liver is immediately below the diaphragm, which would be white on an Xray.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Moving over to the right-hand side of the image, to the left of where the letter L appears, we see the bubble or the convexity of the circle pushing up into that area of white; is that pushing up into the diaphragm?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The top of the stomach is just under the diaphragm, so yes, anatomically, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. So is that a normal or an abnormal radiograph?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think this is unusual. I think this is too much gaseous distension of the stomach than you would expect in a baby in this condition of this age. There is a very small tube, it's difficult to see on this radiograph, but there is a nasogastric tube in.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: A nasogastric tube in the stomach would allow free passage of air usually upwards, so it's unusual to have that degree of gas and we've just seen two previous radiographs with a normal degree of gas on them in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Does this radiograph tell us anything about the infection of the lungs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, you can't see the left lung on this radiograph.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can I move to your joint report then and deal with the conclusions that you have drawn from this series of radiographs, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: My Lord, I'm looking in the joint report at Dr Arthurs' review of the group 3 cases, as he describes them, and paragraph 3 of that report sets out the case of [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What conclusions did you draw overall from this series of radiographs, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can read directly from our joint report, which is that:
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: "Both experts agree that the radiographs show left-sided chest infection, but also marked gaseous dilation of the stomach and the small bowel. Both experts agree there are several potential causes, which would include CPAP belly, sepsis, NEC or exogenous air administration."
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I think that's the main conclusion.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. So, so far as the stomach bubble is concerned, as I'll call it, the possibilities are CPAP belly, someone pumping air in, sepsis and NEC; are they potential causes for this as well?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They are potential causes for dilatation and small bowel dilatation. I think they were not found in this case.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You list a series of possibilities but then there may be other evidence which impacts on whether any of those possibilities remain possibilities?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So they are effectively differential diagnoses for this appearance; that's not to say that they happened in this case.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: No, okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think it was pointed out to you that this particular radiograph showed that there was no gas in the rectum and I think you were asked to comment on whether or not that had any significance in this context.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right. So if you see where the legs are, you can imagine -- if you imagine where the two legs are coming in, in between those would be where the rectum comes out. So an observation has been made that there isn't any gas in that particular location. So that's relevant if [Baby C] were a newborn who had never passed any faeces, meconium, and that this was his first X-ray, because that might suggest that there's a blockage in the bowel.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: As we know, that's not the case. So the presence or absence of gas in a baby who is passing meconium freely has almost no relevance.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we go to the case of [Baby D] next, please, unless there are any other relevant features in your view in the case of [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, that's fine. I think we've covered it.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just before we do, I should have mentioned before evidence was called that at 11 o'clock we will observe the 2 minutes' silence. I can't actually see the digital clock, which will be accurate to the second.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If you can keep an eye on it. When we get to 11 o'clock, we will sit in silence -- you can sit in silence as well, Mr Johnson -- for 2 minutes to observe that silence. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Arthurs, your report in [Baby D]'s case was the same date as that of [Baby C]'s case; is that right.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And again you set out the radiographs that you received in her case; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I want to deal with those next, please, if we may.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is your screen not working?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's not, my Lord, but I'm assisted by my computer which has Professor Arthurs' images.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I would like to adopt the same routine, please, if we may, Dr Arthurs, and identify the pictures in question.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is the first a radiograph of [Baby D], taken on 20 June at 22.22 hours?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: We can see above this one has been typed in red "tile 43". That's just cross-referencing this to the jury's sequence of events.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What do we see or what do you see there, Dr Arthurs, that in any way is abnormal?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's abnormal? Very little. You can see again the heart is white in the middle, the centre blob. Both lungs are black and pretty clear on this radiograph.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Implicitly below that are the diaphragms. The white structure creating a triangle, if you like, on the left of your screen is
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: where the liver would be. Then there is gas in the stomach on the right. And the bones in obviously the skeleton are visible. As far as I can see, I don't think there's an abnormality here.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just for completeness at the bottom left-hand side of the picture, which is the right-hand side of [Baby D], we see part of the bowel?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, yes. Then the small bowel, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So that's 22.22 hours on the 20th.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Moving on to the second picture, which equates to tile 132. This gives us a rather more extensive view, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. This is effectively the whole body, to include the chin, going all the way down to the lower limbs. The main finding here is the --
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Sorry, can we just have a time for this?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I beg your pardon, yes. It's 21 June at 13.32.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's my fault.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So we've moved on to the next day?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. It's about 15 hours, 14 or 15 hours later.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you just talk us through what we can see here, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. There are two features on this radiograph. One is quite obvious and one is quite subtle. The quite obvious one is that the umbilical venous catheter, which is one of the white lines that comes up from the bottom, goes into [Baby D] and then goes up and you can see it goes up into the heart and is kinked. So the comment that we would make on that radiograph is that the UVC has been pushed in too far and needs withdrawing.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The subtler abnormality here is that at the bottom of the patient's right lung, so on the left of the picture, just where it meets the diaphragm, there is a little bit of opacification. I think that was raised at the time as being a right-sided infection and I would agree that could represent a right-sided infection or pneumonia. But you can see the magnitude of that is nothing like what we saw with the previous case.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. The third picture was taken after [Baby D]'s collapse on 22 June at 01.51.27. It equates to tile 216 in the
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: sequence of events. So far as that line that was in the previous picture that was in too far, what do we see, if anything, by contrast in this picture?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: By this time it's clearly been withdrawn and now lies a little bit short of the heart, just under the liver.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So where that triangle of white is on the patient's left, at the top of where the small bowel gas is overlaid.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: It's 10.59.10 at the moment.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. We'll wait for another 35 seconds and then start 2 minutes, but as I say, fortunately the digital clock will tell us to the second.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
It is now 11 o'clock.
(A two-minute silence was observed)
Thank you.
So just going back to this third picture then, please, Dr Arthurs, you told us just before that 2 minutes that the line had clearly been withdrawn.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Can we see the tip of the line there in the middle of a loop almost?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it's in the middle of what looks like a loop, a circular loop, at the top, and actually the tip is within -that's right, that's correct, where the marker is. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is the loop inside the body or is the loop outside the body?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't tell on this radiograph, but it's almost certain to be outside the body.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. So it may well be that the line has been taped on the outside of the body and then --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: -- then it's gone in, okay. Thank you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In fact, there is a sort of rectangular white area. Could that be the tape? You see it below the loop there (indicating).
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It could be. It could just be where the tube overlaps on itself as well, but that's likely to be where the umbilicus and the belly button is. That's right, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is there anything unusual about this appearance?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, I don't think so. Only with reference to the previous radiograph, which showed a little bit of infection at the right lung base, so on the left-hand side of our image, there in fact on that image the diaphragm looks pretty clear.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if that was infection, you could see from the size of it, effectively, that it may have been cleared by that point. So if it was there, it was pretty mild.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. So if the clinical picture was that this was a child who had improved, would the radiographic picture be consistent with that as a proposition?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. There isn't an exact match always with when children get sick and when they have radiographic appearances. What I would say is over the three radiographs that we have, if you were to tell me that this baby was in air for all that time or didn't need any treatment for their infection, that would be consistent.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: We then have a series of radiographs from Alder Hey, which were taken after the death of [Baby D]. I want to move, if we can, rather than looking at them all, because I don't think we need to look at them all -- can we concentrate, Mr Murphy, on page 10 of 14, which is J2380?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If you would, please, Mr Murphy, could you turn this through 90 degrees and make it a bit more visible?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is there anything unusual in this image, please, Dr Arthurs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is a standard lateral radiograph that would have been taken after [Baby D] died. So instead of being taken from the front, it would have been taken through the side. You can see the spine at the bottom and you can see the bowel gas, the bubbly circles which are black.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The umbilical venous catheter is still in and you can see that as the tube that comes in from the top and goes down. What's
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: striking about this radiograph is the line just in front of the vertebral bodies, just in front of the spine. So there is a black line that follows from left to right. If you could magnify that portion that might help.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So there's a black line that follows immediately in front of the spine. It's black because there is air and that's where the two main big blood vessels in the body are, the aorta and the IVC.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So just -- these are all your daily work -- the aorta is what, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The aorta is the big blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood to all the organs in the body and they return, through a large vein called the inferior vena cava, back to the heart.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So out through the artery, return through the vein?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Through the vein, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is this in effect the main highway of the plumbing of the circulation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, and there are two big vessels that run up and down the body, the aorta and the vena cava.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Protected from behind by the spine?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: From the front by?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Everything else.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Exactly, yes. Well designed! So what can we see in whichever -- can you tell the difference on this quality of image as to which of the two it is?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's not about the quality, it's the fact that both tubes would overlie each other if you were to take the image in this plane. So I can't tell which of those tubes effectively the gas is within.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What is the significance of that amount of gas, if any?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The significance, as I think I've presented already in this courtroom, is that that is an unusual appearance and that is not a typical appearance that we see in children who have died without an explanation.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What potential mechanisms is that amount of gas consistent with?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that amount of gas has been seen previously in babies who have died of sepsis, overwhelming infection. It's also seen in sudden unexpected death in infancy, in trauma, road traffic accidents and the like. And it is also seen in two of the other children in this case.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Is one of the other two [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, who we reviewed, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: We'll leave the third for in due course.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is this case, in other words the case of [Baby D], the other case that you were referring to when you gave evidence about [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: That this was the only time you'd seen more air in a child than in the case of [Baby A]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is this appearance consistent with somebody injecting air into a child?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I think that's one of the explanations that needs to be considered.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Have you ever come across a baby with this amount of gas in the great vessels for which no cause was found?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Did you reach a conclusion, on the basis of the clinical history, as to what was the most likely or the most plausible explanation for this appearance?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the absence of any evidence that suggested that [Baby D] had died of overwhelming sepsis or any of the other explanations that we've put forward, I considered that the radiographs are consistent with, but not diagnostic of, external intravenous air administration.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Would you wait there, please? I'm sure there will be some more questions for you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS

Professor Arthurs, if it's all right with you and with everybody, it's probably most sensible if I deal with [Baby D] first since we've just been looking at her and we've got your evidence on that, and then we'll have a look at [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So dealing with [Baby D] first of all, is it right that when you looked at the post-mortem images of [Baby D], you identified normal post-mortem gas dilation in places where you would normally expect to find it?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's reasonable, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And that includes intracranial, so in the head area?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: That might be a generalisation, but there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Intracardiac, so in the heart region. And also bowel?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'll ask you about the image we've looked at, we don't need to go back to it, we've just seen it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As for where that gas or that air was, is it right that it could be either in the aorta or in the IVC or in both, it's just difficult to tell because of how the structures lie?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So it's one or both of the great vessels as it's put.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Now, we looked at the question of the significance of gas in the abdominal vessels when you were last giving evidence, Professor Arthurs, and I don't propose to go back through all of that. I might just rehearse some key points and see if you agree or disagree.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But as a starting point would it be right to say that, generally, the significance of gas in the large abdominal vessels at post-mortem isn't known?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's reasonable.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And when you last gave evidence, we looked at, and you were kind enough to look at with me, the work that you had done with cases at Great Ormond Street to try to assess how often one might find gas in those abdominal vessels post-mortem.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You found, on the survey that you were able to conduct, in about 25% of the cases, there was gas that could be described as post-mortem gas?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In about a quarter of cases we found that gas was in those locations --
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- for which there was typically an explanation, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You've got the histories of what had happened and you found gas in about a quarter, however we characterise that, and that could be considered to be post-mortem gas?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So for that reason, subject to the history in [Baby D]'s case, it is possible for this to be post-mortem gas?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it is post-mortem gas in the sense that it's gas that we're seeing after the baby has died on a radiograph, so yes. The question here is whether it's explained, is maybe what you're getting at.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: When I'm referring to post-mortem gas like this, and the jury recall when we dealt with it lat time, there are natural processes, once a body has died, that lead to gas appearing in the various parts of the body?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And that's what you and I are referring to earlier when I mentioned about intracranial, intracardiac and bowel gas?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And so with the study that you did where you say you identified a quarter of them where there was gas, that was explicable as natural gas built up post-mortem?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, so I think that I need to clarify that. We often see gas in different locations, as you've described, as a normal feature in normal babies who have died. We see those on postmortem X-rays.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The 25% was referring to in how many babies do we see gas in those great vessels if we were to go back and look through a
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: large number. Having done that, in how many of those was there an explanation or was there no explanation forthcoming? And that's where I gave evidence to say that we saw that typically, so in those particular locations, usually attributable to causes such as infection, sudden unexpected death in infancy, road traffic accidents.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes, but the gas you're describing is a post-mortem build-up of gas in those cases?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So subject to the clinical history in [Baby D]'s case, it is possible for this to be natural post-mortem gas but it depends on what the explanations are and the history?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. As for the possible explanations for this that may arise, and one has to consider that in the whole picture, air administration from outside is one possibility?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And that could either be deliberate or accidental, depending on all the circumstances?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I presume so, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I've asked you about post-mortem gas. Other possibilities that you acknowledged, and in fact we looked at some of these last time when you gave evidence, was the result of sepsis or infection. I know you're nodding, but you have to say yes or no for the transcript to picks it up.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, if there's evidence of overwhelming infection, then that could be at attributed to that.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You were also able to explain that where there has been resuscitation, CPR, that also can lead to gas emerging in the great vessels?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, we don't think that resuscitation causes gas, but we think that the normal gas that's in the post-mortem state could be re-circulated if there's vigorous cardiac resuscitation. That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So it encourages the gas to come out of solution in the blood, in effect?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think it more redistributes the gas, in effect.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Redistributes, all right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So depending on the history, those are all things that can go to explain why it is that we see the gas?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Radiographs are supportive of but not diagnostic of air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not air embolus, so --
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Exogenous air administration?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: These are images that show you where the gas is. The images can't give you an explanation, but the clinical history can.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So there may be a number of explanations but one of them is exogenous air administration?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you, Professor Arthurs, that's what I wanted to ask about [Baby D]'s case.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask next about [Baby C]. Just to clarify one or two matters, the first image I would like to ask you about was the X-ray we saw and it's in the bundle of X-rays for [Baby C] and it was the one -- I think it's page 2, Mr Murphy -- which is 10 June 2015 at 22.38.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it's the second one we looked at.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It was the second, thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: This is an X-ray, the second X-ray taken that day of [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Page 1 was the first one. You identified for us -- is it the left-sided consolidation in the lung?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: In the left lung, thank you. Did you regard that as consistent with a clinical sign of infection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Was it your view, again depending on all the clinical factors we bear in mind, that a left-sided chest infection could
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: be a significant factor in the death of a severely growth restricted baby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that was the conclusion I came to.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I would like to ask you next about the following photograph, which is at page 3 -- I say photograph, sorry, radiograph. That was for 12 June at 12.36.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just a few questions about this, please, Professor Arthurs. When you were asked about the findings in the joint report, you agreed that this included left-sided chest infection and also marked gaseous dilation of the stomach and the small bowel.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just as to that and the question of the dilation of stomach and small bowel, it can sometimes be a little difficult, can't it, to distinguish the small from the large bowel? Maybe not for you, but can it be difficult to distinguish small from large?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not quite sure that I can comment. I think others may find it difficult to distinguish between areas of bowel, that's correct, but this is the type of thing I do every day in my clinical practice.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So you're able to say with some degree of certainty that what we see here is marked gaseous dilation of the stomach and the small bowel?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Do you want me to explain the...?
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I don't want to hold you back if there's a relevant explanation, but there's no challenge from me as to your description in that way.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I don't challenge what you say about that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As for the cause of the dilation, or possible causes of this dilation, on 12 June, subject to the overall picture, what you considered was, first of all, whether there's any question of NEC. That can be an explanation but that depends on all the circumstances and whether we find other evidence of NEC?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The comment was made, looking at this radiograph, by some of the other experts that there's lucency on the left-hand side of the image as we're looking at it.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So the big circle of black at the top is stomach.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The multiple sausages, if you like, of black going through on the right-hand side are small bowel. And then there is an area on the -- of smaller bits of black and white on the left-hand side of the abdomen. So there was a comment made about that this could be pneumatosis, which is gas within the bowel wall, which is a feature of necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So I think they're referring to two separate things and so I refer to the distension of the stomach and the small bowel as being important.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And the possibility of NEC along the flank has been raised on that radiograph, but as far as I know, no NEC was found in [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I'm just going through the possible things. So that's one of them.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sepsis or infection can explain what we see here; that's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: It's possible that some sort of obstruction or twist in the gut could account for this. Just pausing there, when you gave evidence to the jury earlier, you explained that in a situation like that it's relevant as to whether or not there has been faeces or meconium passing out of a baby.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: If the bowels have been opened and therefore faeces or, perhaps if it's a very newborn baby, meconium has passed out, that would not be consistent with an obstruction because it would suggest there's been movement through the bowel?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right, it's not consistent with an inherited obstruction.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Obviously, if one of the findings is that the bowels have not been opened over that period, then that possibility becomes one for further consideration?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So I think this baby is 4 days old at the point that this has been done.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So as you know, when we're asked to perform radiographs, we're given a clinical history as to why that should be done to justify it. So a baby who hasn't had his bowels open for 4 days, that would be in the clinical history as to is there an obstruction on this radiograph.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I don't think this is the clinical scenario that we're talking about here.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: It may be, actually, Professor Arthurs, about no bowels opened and we've been through that, we have access to that, which is why I keep it within the area you can deal with, which is depending on the clinical history it may be consistent or may not be consistent with an obstruction.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A further explanation for what we see on this image is excessive administration of air via the NGT, the nasogastric tube. And one other possible explanation for what we see here, depending on all the circumstances, is what we understand is called CPAP belly. Is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, because both of those are a way of introducing air into the stomach.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes, right. CPAP belly is when air, in effect being blown in through the CPAP system, has accumulated in the stomach and passed into the bowel and in effect inflates it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Technically, that's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Can I just ask one final question and it's just to do with the photograph -- the image, sorry, we looked at, before this one, the image at page 2. When you were giving evidence initially, you described that we could see the NGT in the stomach; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is that the tube or the white line that appears to have a coil in it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right. It's coiled in that direction in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is that coiled because as it is put down into the stomach, it's a thin, small tube and it rolls round as it's put inside?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a bendy flexible tube, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: All right. Thank you, Professor Arthurs.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR JOHNSON
Can we go back to radiograph number 3 for [Baby C], please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You were going to give us an explanation for why it is, Dr Arthurs, that you can be sure that this is the small bowel as opposed to the large bowel that is inflated; could you tell us?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Anatomically, the small bowel is free to move around, so when you distend it full of gas, gas rises, so it lifts it up. So typically the area you'll see a small bowel full of gas is in the middle, as we can see in this image.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The large bowel is fixed to the outside of the abdomen, ascending on one side and descending on the other, so the gas that you see on the outside of the flanks, effectively, and the outer peripheries of the bowel is large bowel.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So it's not that difficult to look at this image and to say, gosh, the stomach's dilated and then there's some gas that's gone through into the small bowel and the large bowel is not dilated.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. I think someone used the word mesentery at some stage as to the fixing of the large bowel.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The mesentery is the blood supply to the small bowel and the large bowel. It's like an apron, almost, that feeds the bowel.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. The issue of bowel obstruction: is another word for that volvulus?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: These are all different ways in which the bowel can be blocked. One of the ways which you have to consider in newborn babies is a blockage they were born with, a congenital obstruction, and that can occur at any level. It can occur above the stomach, just below the stomach, at any one of a number of different levels through the bowel.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You can imagine if the bowel was blocked at a particular level, you see air dilated above that point and the stomach and wherever else. So it gives you a marker of where it could be that the bowel is blocked.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Do we have any such marker on this image?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: If there was a blockage in the bowel, is that something -- given the date of this image, which is a day or two before [Baby C] died, would one expect the blockage, if it was there, to be found at a post-mortem examination?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: More commonly it will be found before the baby dies. So babies get -- we know this is a common clinical occurrence, we know babies are born with obstructions.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: They tend to block very early in the first 12, 24, 48 hours. They have an X-ray which looks like there's a blockage with gas in the middle and nothing below.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: They then don't pass any meconium and they go to theatre for an operation.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And I think in one of the other cases that we discuss here, that's exactly what happened. So small bowel congenital obstruction is a well-recognised, well-documented medical occurrence.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Is there any evidence for that on these images?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. Not on the imaging, not really on the clinical history, and none was found at autopsy, as far as I am aware.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So is it a credible explanation for [Baby C] having problems, a bowel blockage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, not a congenital inherited bowel blockage.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The other term that you raised was volvulus, which is where the bowel twists on itself. Of course that isn't an inherited blockage. That can happen in small babies. You can sometimes get this sort of appearance where, if the bowel twists on itself, you'll get blockage above that point, so you would get gas in the small bowel and the stomach above that point.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Again, that's often a surgical emergency, the baby will go to theatre, they may not survive the surgery, but certainly that would be found, documented and documented at autopsy.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So if that possibility existed, again it would be found if there was a post-mortem examination?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I would expect that to happen.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did, because in my working life, day to day, I attend caesarean sections, particularly emergency caesarean sections, which most consultants wouldn't normally do, certainly for term babies. But I do and I know that parents, especially first-time parents, are desperately keen that have their baby with them as soon as possible. So babies who are in good condition are given to their parents to have what we've already heard of as skin-to-skin, which has a lot of positive benefits to parents.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I mean no disrespect to [Baby D]'s parents at all here, quite often, particularly with first-time parents, they're not very confident about the way they hold babies and babies can easily put their chin on to their chest and have their head flop forward. If they do that, that can collapse slightly their windpipe because, unlike in adults where the windpipe is fairly rigid, in babies it's not formed as a complete circle, so can collapse. And I see this fairly regularly -- it's usually a dad that alerts us to the fact that the baby looks a funny colour and it's usually because the baby's popped their chin on their chest, and once you reposition the baby -- and sometimes you may need to give inflation breaths -- the baby appears fine.

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So equally consistent with an inexperienced dad?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Oh, yes. Yes, and I mean that in no disrespectful way at all.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: On behalf of the dads of this world, I forgive you! The grunting that you recorded, is that uncommon after a C-section delivery?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, not at all. Babies who are born by caesarean section retain lung fluid, so the babies' airway when it's inside mum is full of fluid, and if babies come out the usual way, their chest
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: has a big squash as it comes out of the birth canal and so that fluid is expelled.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When babies are born by caesarean section that doesn't happen and so a lot of fluid can be retained. And that can be one of the causes that babies grunt after birth.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Infection is another, but it's commonly called TTN, which means transient tachypnoea of the newborn. That means transient increased breathing rate of the newborn and it usually resolves itself within 24 hours or so.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You move on at paragraph 5.4 of your report to record the fact that [Baby D] continued to grunt and that was coincident with a drop in her temperature to 36.3 degrees. What conclusion or opinion did you reach from that combination of circumstances?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Newborn babies with an infection don't necessarily have a temperature in the way that adults and older children do. In fact it's probably more common for them to get cold and not be able to maintain their temperature. So a temperature of 36.3 is indicating to me that [Baby D] was not able to maintain her temperature and that, in association with grunting, would make me worried that she had -- she was developing an infection or had an ongoing infection.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And should [Baby D] have been screened at that stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: She certainly should have been screened at that stage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did a review eventually take place when [Baby D] refused to feed and had poor colour?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The review took place subsequently, a bit later, when she refused to feed, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Was it that that led to her admission to the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In general terms were the investigations undertaken by Dr Brunton and others in the neonatal unit appropriate and was the treatment that was given to [Baby D] appropriate?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You move on to note the fact that [Baby D]'s temperature rose to 39 degrees. Her heart rate also rose. She
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: was in an incubator and the nursing records suggested that the temperature was set at -- I don't think you record the actual rate it was set at, but you draw a conclusion as to whether or not it was too high. Could you tell us about that, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Newborn babies, if they're well, and they're born at term, usually maintain their temperature reasonably well, unlike premature babies. So the nursing staff in a neonatal unit are very used to premature babies coming into the unit and needing to be kept warm, so they will set the incubator quite high in order for that to happen. Term babies don't need to have the temperature on the incubator quite so high because they're usually okay at maintaining their temperature.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think probably what happened here is because when [Baby D] arrived, her temperature was low at 37.3, the nursing staff increased the incubator temperature in an attempt to raise [Baby D]'s temperature back to the normal range, but I think probably they overdid it and so her temperature went up and her heart rate went up correspondingly, which is what you'd expect. Then when they turned down the incubator, her temperature stabilised again.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Okay. So in terms of inferring from those circumstances whether or not the rise in temperature was related to infection or to environmental issues --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think it was environmental. I think it was iatrogenic. I think it was caused by the high incubator temperature.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Could you give us that long word again?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Iatrogenic. It means somebody caused it.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Okay. Outside influences?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think it's in the glossary.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did [Baby D] continue to improve on CPAP?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, she did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think at that stage, so we're now talking about the early -- sorry, no, I think she was needing 50% oxygen at that stage; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, she was, she was needing 50% oxygen. She improved when she was put on to CPAP but she still required around 50% oxygen, so quite a high oxygen requirement.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What about her corresponding respiratory rate at that stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Her respiratory rate was high. So two things going on: she needed oxygen, quite a lot of oxygen, and her respiratory rate was above normal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And is that the reason why the decision appears to have been taken to intubate and ventilate [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Breathing at that rate is hard work for babies, and therefore rather than wait for babies to get tired, if you can see that they are working hard and their oxygen requirement and their respiratory rate is high, it's much safer and better for the baby to intervene and offer the baby the next stage of respiratory support rather than wait for the baby to collapse and then offer that respiratory support. So the clinicians looking at her just felt that she would tire if she was left to continue breathing at that high rate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We have seen this morning the chest X-ray that was taken following [Baby D]'s intubation. But what conclusions did you draw from that X-ray, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I thought the X-ray showed evidence of some retained lung fluid, but I didn't think it showed evidence of infection.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What did you think about the clinical picture?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The clinical picture of [Baby D], I felt, was consistent -- the clinical picture was consistent with infection, even though the X-ray wasn't. That was because her white cell count, which is a marker of infection, was high, and within the white cells of the body are a number of different sorts of white cells. In [Baby D]'s case her neutrophil count was high, and that is usually indicative of a bacterial-type infection, and that was high in [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Okay. We've heard that the C-reactive protein reading was normal, but we've also heard many times that that doesn't mean that there isn't a problem; do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. You can't look at that in isolation, you have to look at it in the round with the clinical picture and the patient in front of you.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The following morning at 9 am, [Baby D] was extubated, the ET tube removed, and attempts were made to put in a line through the -- put in lines, I should say, through the umbilicus; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You refer to the fact that the arterial line was in the wrong place and had to be removed and that the venous line had to be pulled back as referred to by Dr Arthurs from the radiographs.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You in effect express a view consistent with what Dr Arthurs has told us, that the X-ray shows evidence of infection in the lower right of [Baby D]'s lungs; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right. There's a small patch of consolidation or infection.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In summary, what conclusion did you reach as to [Baby D]'s progress and status between being extubated at 9 o'clock in the morning and her first collapse at about 1.30 the following morning?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, she was well and stable. She needed some help with her breathing in terms of CPAP, but that was in air and her saturations were normal. So the observations were also normal. So this was a baby who was improving.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, she clearly had an infection, had a pneumonia, but she had responded to treatment and was improving. So she wasn't cured of her pneumonia, she clearly still had it, but had improved and was getting better.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We heard evidence that the decision was taken by Dr Brunton to start feeding [Baby D] with breast milk.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What does that tell us as to [Baby D]'s progress?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, you wouldn't want to start feeding a baby who was unstable in any way, and I'm sure if Dr Brunton felt that she was likely to deteriorate and need to go back on the ventilator, he wouldn't have started feeds at that time. So the fact that he made that decision indicates to me that she was stable.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. You refer next to [Baby D]'s collapses.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Could you tell the jury what you took into account and what you found to be significant so far as those collapses were concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The thing that was striking about the collapses were that they were -- all three of them were sudden and unexpected
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: because, as I've just stated, [Baby D], certainly prior to the first collapse, was stable and even after the first collapse she recovered very well.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So these were collapses that came out of the blue, they weren't expected, there was nothing leading up to them that would make people concerned. The collapses were sudden.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She recovered very quickly with the first two episodes, sadly not with the third. And two of the episodes were associated with an unusual mottling of the skin. So these -- all the episodes were perplexing to me and didn't have any clear cause.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you find [Baby D]'s recoveries after the first two -- the nature and speed of her recoveries after the first two incidents to be of any significance?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: She seemed to recover very quickly once the team resuscitated her or give her intervention -- not resuscitation, they gave her intervention -- and she recovered remarkably quickly and was back to being stable again if you look at her observations.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as the -- I'm looking at your paragraph 5.14 now.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as the second episode was concerned, was there anything unusual about that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, it's reported from the nursing staff present that she became very distressed and was crying, and it's common in term babies who are put on to CPAP that they will often fight the CPAP machine, they find it uncomfortable, because whether it's given by mask or prongs, you have to develop a seal in order to administer CPAP and that can be uncomfortable. So premature babies, if they're ill or term babies if they're ill, will often just lie there and allow CPAP to be administered. But a baby who is relatively well and feisty will fight the CPAP and will become upset.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that is a known fact. But [Baby D] had not previously been upset on CPAP, she'd allowed the CPAP to be given, so the fact that she became upset then was a concern to me. She had tolerated CPAP well prior to that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as the undoubted infection that [Baby D] had, did you reach a conclusion as to whether that been acquired before birth or after birth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think this was a congenital infection and it was acquired before birth.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But having acquired that infection, how did you view [Baby D]'s progress once she'd been admitted to the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, [Baby D] became unwell in the hours after birth.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think the administration of antibiotics was late, but once she got to the neonatal unit, she was investigated and treated appropriately.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Was [Baby D]'s presentation, as recorded by the treating medical staff, consistent with that of a baby on a path of deterioration who was going to be dead within a few hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. No, [Baby D] didn't give -- the clinical team knew that she had an infection and I can review her notes and I can see that she's got an infection, but there was nothing to indicate that death was imminent.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In the context specifically of pneumonia, how did you summarise [Baby D]'s position, please? I'm looking at your paragraph 5.17.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, I can read that, I said:
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Although [Baby D] had pneumonia [and as far as I know no one is questioning that, I don't think], she was clinically well, she was in air and had normal blood gases. She had no respiratory compromise at all and this is not the picture of a baby with a pneumonia severe enough to kill her."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just so that the jury can understand, what is the typical picture of a baby with a pneumonia severe enough to kill them that ends in death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Usually babies will show a gradual decline and deterioration and an increase in the kind of care that they need. So their respiratory rate will continue to climb, they will not tolerate being on CPAP and their blood gases will decline, so they will need to move from CPAP to more invasive ventilation. Their blood parameters will alter and become abnormal. They may need extra drugs to help with their blood pressure. So there is an altogether slow clinical decline rather than a sudden collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What conclusion did you draw as to the likely mechanism by which [Baby D]'s collapse had been provoked?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, taking into account the suddenness of the collapses, the very quick recovery of two of them, I was clear
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: that this wasn't the infection that had caused the collapse. So I was looking at something else and the something else had to be something unusual and something odd. And of course, the clinical condition also showed us that she had episodes of this unusual skin discolouration, which the medical team described.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And excluding other things -- we all make a differential diagnosis and you cross off things that don't fit with that clinical picture and the scenario that's put before you. So I excluded lots of other things and came to the conclusion that [Baby D] had air administered to her and that was the cause of the collapses.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And by what -- into what part of her had the air been administered to cause these collapses?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, intravenous air, either through the UVC or the peripheral cannula that she had in her hand.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: A question may occur to the jury as to, if that is the mechanism in all three instances, why did she recover so quickly from two and die on the third occasion? And can you provide an answer to that conundrum?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can speculate as to why I think that, which is obviously what you're asking me.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We know from animal studies that with air embolus, it's the volume of gas and the speed at which it is delivered that is fatal or can prove fatal. So I think if the volume in the first two cases, the volume of air administered was small, that wouldn't have been enough to kill [Baby D]. But what we do know is if a large volume of gas is administered into a vein, when it gets to the right side of the heart, if the volume is sufficient, it causes a gas lock within the heart and then causes sudden circulatory collapse. And I think probably that is what was the ultimate issue with [Baby D] with the third collapse in that the volume of air was larger than it had been previously and caused the circulation to stop.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is there any other feature of [Baby D]'s presentation over those three collapses that you identified as being consistent with your conclusion that this was a case of air being introduced to [Baby D]'s circulation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The suddenness of the collapse, which was completely unexpected given the preceding clinical picture. In two of the cases she was resuscitated. In two of the cases there was the very graphic skin discolouration, which does fit with previous
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: cases of air embolus seen in adults and to a lesser extent in children. And of course, there's then also the issue of air in the great vessels found on post-mortem radiographs.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Bohin. I'm sure there will be more questions for you, if you'd wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS

Dr Bohin, I just want to understand why you're saying, and go over this with you, [Baby D]'s cause of death is air embolus. You have said in the absence of infection, that something else had to be unusual and odd.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Something else killed [Baby D], which I felt was unusual and odd.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You said taking into account sudden collapse and quick recoveries, if not infection, that something else had to be unusual and odd.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. That's your starting point, looking for something unusual and odd; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I wasn't looking for something unusual and odd. I'd already looked at the clinical picture and excluded things. Once I'd excluded conditions in my differential diagnosis, commoner things, they'd been excluded so I was left then with something unusual and odd.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You said to the jury:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "There were episodes of discolouration. Excluding other things I concluded air administration caused collapse."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's what you said to begin with; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So looking for something unusual and odd, episodes of discolouration, excluding other things, that led you to air administration; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You also went on to add that it was sudden. That was something you bore in mind?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You've also made reference to air in the great vessels?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But that's a matter we've heard from Owen Arthurs. I'm not going to ask you about that, there's various explanations for that, aren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Dr Arthurs has already given his evidence on that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think potential explanations.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Potential explanations.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You also at the end, dealing with this, said to the jury she was resuscitated twice.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can you explain why does resuscitating her twice have anything to do with demonstrating this is an air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She did actually correct herself.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I said intervention.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You said resuscitate to being with.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And then I said intervention. I said that's probably a poor term, that she required intervention on the first two episodes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We'll be coming to the terminology in a little bit. Whether intervention or resuscitation, why should that go to pick out air embolus rather than something else causing her desaturation?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Because I'd already excluded other causes for the collapses.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We'll look a bit more closely at some of what you said to us. But before I do, can I just confirm this: you made reference to [Baby D] being distressed at one point in your evidence, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that of any relevance, are you suggesting?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It can be, in cases of children on CPAP, which I explained, but it can also be a feature of children or adults -not children, adults -- who have received air embolus. They can become distressed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Of adults. What's the basis of applying that to a neonate in the position [Baby D] was in?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The literature, as I think I said when I last gave evidence, is very poor on this and most of the literature is based on what researchers have seen in adults. There's very, very little on children. So it may be that they also get distressed in the same way that adults do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But the literature is poor?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So there's a poor basis in terms of saying that a baby that gets distressed is getting distressed because of an air embolus, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Babies can get distressed for all number of things and air embolus is one of those things, in my opinion.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In your opinion, but in fact you are speculating when you say that if adults get distressed that may be a cause of distress for a neonate in this position, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But most of the opinion is based on evidence that is in the literature and very little of it relates to neonates. Very little.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And neonates have different systems from adults, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not as far as I'm aware, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You're a consultant neonatologist, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Isn't there a reason why we have specialist neonatologists?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You can't just apply what you get with adults and say, "This must apply to babies, newborn babies", can you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, I thought the question was that babies had different systems to adults and I said no because I don't think they do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is it biological systems, is that what you understood it to be --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- that it was suggested that babies were different from adults biologically?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think perhaps a bit clearer as to what you're suggesting.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Neonatal babies may have different physiological systems from adults, mightn't they?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: They don't have different systems; their physiology may be different from adults, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What applies to adults may not necessarily apply to neonates?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But it may.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But you need to have a basis to see that before you assert that it does, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A lot of what we do in medicine in neonates relates to what people have previously done in adults. So for a lot of the care we give to neonates there is no neonatal basis for it at all.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Neonates may get distressed for very many reasons, mightn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I said that, yes.
