blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the levels of distress and the causes may be different from adults, mightn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They might be but they might also be the same.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. So what is your basis for saying that if adults get distressed by an air embolus, that is a reason for why [Baby D] was crying on this occasion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't say that that was the only reason. I said that was part of the constellation of features.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm looking at that particular feature and asking you: what is the basis for saying that is why she was getting distressed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because in my opinion that forms part of what -- how an air embolus can present.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So do you disregard what the treating doctors and nurses say about the CPAP having upset her?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't disregard it.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So it's in fact consistent with CPAP upsetting her, the distress; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: CPAP hadn't upset her before. But it had -- she appeared distressed on that second occasion. But for the time she was on CPAP before, it hadn't upset her, which was why I came to the conclusion that actually she was quite content on CPAP.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Let us understand what you're saying. On the one hand, you're taking some research that applies to adults who are distressed with an air embolus and you're saying that may show why [Baby D] was upset; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Possibly, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And on the other hand you're saying when the physician and the nurses say that they thought it was because she was upset on CPAP, they may have got that wrong in fact?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think the nurses -- none of the nurses said she was upset on CPAP. I think it was -- one of the registrars, I think Dr Brunton, made a decision to take her off CPAP because he thought that that might be making her upset. And that was after she had recovered from the second incident, so he didn't see her distressed on CPAP. He took her off because he thought it might be contributing to her distress, as far as I remember.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: One moment, please. I don't mean to be rude.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)
In any event, you say that may be wrong when it is said that she was distressed because of CPAP?
I don't know who said she was distressed. Dr Brunton took her off CPAP because she may be distressed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I don't see anybody wrote that she was distressed on CPAP.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did she continue to be distressed when she'd been taken off CPAP?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: With crying and being --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There's no suggestion she did, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We know there's a period during which Caroline Oakley performed various cares, aren't there, with [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And we know that period to some extent runs up to the point of the third collapse, don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And at no other point do we hear anything about [Baby D] being distressed, do we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We don't hear about [Baby D] getting distressed before the first collapse either, do we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, she was stable of CPAP then.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the one occasion that we have [Baby D] being distressed is the one occasion when the treating physician was of the view it could be the CPAP distressing her?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that wasn't what he said.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It coincides with the point when she was taken off CPAP because of concerns that it was distressing her, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I'm sorry, I can't agree with that. He took her off CPAP after the second event, after she'd recovered from the second event, because what had been reported to him prior to the second event was that she was upset on CPAP and he therefore took the decision to take her off in case CPAP was upsetting her. He didn't review it. It was something that was put to him by the nursing staff, so that was his way of treating her then, but in response to what he'd been told by the nursing staff.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He didn't see that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Don't you accept that someone there said she should come off CPAP because she was distressed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, he said she should come off CPAP in case the CPAP was distressing her. He didn't see it. It was a therapeutic intervention that he thought might help [Baby D], but he hadn't seen it first-hand.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So in terms of air embolus making a neonate cry, she doesn't cry on event number 1, does she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She doesn't cry on event number 3?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And we're clear she is crying at a time when someone decided to take the decision to take her off CPAP in case CPAP upset her?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, she wasn't crying when she was taken off CPAP. She had recovered from the second event by the time she was taken off CPAP. She wasn't crying at that stage; she was crying prior to the second event.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Are you just trying to find any available detail actually to support this air embolus theory, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, absolutely not.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Because if you're right, we might expect to see distress on each occasion, mightn't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, because the clinical presentation of air embolus is variable and, as I said in my previous evidence, you don't need to have every single element of -- every single clinical sign of air embolus for there to be an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You just take whatever bits are available and try and work them into your theory, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I absolutely don't.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you have seized on this distress, that the clinicians have linked to the CPAP and you are just working it in, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And not only are you doing that, but you are basing it on research you say to do with adults, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm basing it on the available research on adults, children and animals --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You told us adults.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- that is available. I looked at all the research that is easily available and there's very little on neonates.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Discolouration. Discolouration can be caused by conditions other than air embolus, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There can be many different reasons, can't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes./
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You don't actually know what the discolouration on [Baby D] was like? You don't know, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You haven't seen it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I haven't.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You don't have a picture or a photograph of it, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We have various descriptions from witnesses dealing with this. You cannot say whether what one witness is describing they saw on one occasion with one child is the same as what another witness is saying on another occasion with another child? There's no way of knowing that, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You cannot say, or you do not say, what discolouration is specifically distinctive of an air embolus, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Or do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. So any discolouration then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Come on, tell us then. Which one?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, which one what?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Help us: which discolouration indicates an air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The discolouration described by the clinical staff, both the nurses and the doctors who saw [Baby D], the patchy discolouration that came and went is compatible with an air embolus, taking into account the clinical situation that we had.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But we know there are lots of different discolourations that may be exhibited by a neonate for many different reasons, don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Neonates can get discolouration, they can get rashes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: None of the known discolourations or rashes that I have seen in a neonate are anything like approaching what was described by the clinical staff treating [Baby D]. Now, I wasn't there and obviously I didn't have -- there hasn't been a photograph taken of it, so like everyone else, I'm left to glean information from what the clinicians wrote at the time. And what they wrote at the time is not compatible with any other known pathology that I know of in a neonate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No, and right at the beginning of dealing with you and Mr Evans in cross-examination, Dr Evans, in the questioning, I identified a number of possibilities in cases where medical opinion is called for. One of them is it may be not possible to identify a particular cause, for example. Do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. So there may be various explanations for what happens, it may not always be immediately clear what explanation applies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If you're going to use discolouration as a way of identifying an air embolus, we need to have something which marks that out as an air embolus rather than anything else.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not using discolouration alone. As I've already said, it's the constellation of features, not just of the clinical discolouration, although that absolutely forms a part of it, because what has been described by clinicians, quite consistently, does not fit with any other known pathological process that I have seen in a neonate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What I would like you to help us with is what makes it fit specifically with air embolus rather than whatever else may be out there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because those type of skin lesions have been previously described in air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What description are we looking for that marks it out?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We're looking for these patchy -- not mottling, I won't use that term because that will confuse people into thinking that mottling that we see in babies when they are in extremis for other reasons -- these were -- in some cases they were described as tracking lesions, in some cases they were described as circular/oval lesions with a reddy-brown discolouration that came and went.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You're telling us what various practitioners have described to us. I'm asking you to help us with what specific presentation are we meant to be measuring that against that shows it as an air embolus rather than anything else or even anything unknown?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There is no single diagnostic feature of an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What about the discolouration, I'm asking you, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can only go on what other people have described in their series(?), in adults and in children, where skin lesions have been identified, and they describe similar lesions.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So there is no presentation of discolouration that we can use that establishes that is an air embolus that you can point to?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, in the Lee and Tanswell paper that we discussed last time, the cases there where there was skin discolouration was described -- sorry.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You carry on.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In that paper the skin discolouration described was remarkably similar to the skin discolouration described by the clinicians here.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can we put up, please, page 24946. It's a J number.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Could we enlarge the section which has the highlighting over it, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We looked at this before, so we're familiar with it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Out of the 50 or so cases, and there are four or five of them, 11%, where discolouration was identified and it was described, from this one study as:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Blanching and migrating areas of cutaneous pallor were noted in several cases and in one of our own cases we noted bright pink vessels against a generally cyanosed cutaneous background."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what we have in the description in particular of one case from this study; do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: First of all, we have had many different descriptions across the children where air embolus is alleged in this case so far. They do not conform or all conform to this, do they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think they're pretty similar.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Nowhere in the clinical notes or in the clinical notes for any of the children that we have seen have we seen anyone talking about "bright pink vessels against a generally cyanosed cutaneous background". We haven't seen that description in any clinical note made at the time, have we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We've seen brown, reddy-brown patches on a background of a child that's cyanosed. So I think we have.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've seen "dark brown +++ tracking", haven't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's not this description, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it is, because tracking could be against the vessels so --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Could be?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Have you seen anything that matches this with any degree of precision?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think it's fairly similar to be honest.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You think dark brown is similar to this? "Dark brown/black across the trunk" is in the notes from Dr Brunton for the first time [Baby D] collapsed.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We can see what's there and I suggest to you that doesn't conform to dark brown tracking across the trunk.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think what we're looking at here are the features that -- you can get skin discolouration with an air embolus. I think the actual details of that, they've described their case and the clinical team here have described what they've seen in [Baby D]'s case. So there is skin discolouration.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We can take this down, Mr Murphy, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You, Dr Bohin, are using just various descriptions of discolouration and saying it's air embolus without any precision at all, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I'm absolutely not. I'm looking at the case as a whole. I'm trying to find out why [Baby D] collapsed on three occasions and was not resuscitable on the third.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree we in fact have no particular presentation to measure this against, do we, the colour of an air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, could you rephrase the question?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Would you agree there's no uniform presentation to measure this against?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's no uniform presentation. We can only go on what others have seen and reported in the literature. It's rare, so no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the only description you point to in the literature, which you have raised just then, is that one description we've seen in Lee and Tanswell, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you agree -- well, that's the one you point to.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We've got three distinct events with [Baby D] in the early hours of the morning on 22 June, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: One at 1.30, one at 3 o'clock, one at 3.45; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've had a description of a vivid discolouration on the first one of those, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I make it plain, I suggest to you that does not match the description in Lee and Tanswell; you say it does.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I say they're remarkably similar, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm not going to keep repeating that, but [Baby D] makes a full and relatively rapid recovery on that occasion, doesn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've seen in the notes a less marked discolouration on the second event, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And [Baby D] makes a full and a relatively rapid recovery, doesn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, she does.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Sadly, the third event, which did result in death, there was no evidence of any discolouration at all, was there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Now, if these are three distinct incidents, it follows when we look at that third incident, discolouration provides no basis for identifying cause of death on that occasion, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Discolouration doesn't, but there are other features that in my opinion do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She isn't distressed on the third occasion, is she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There is no discolouration on the third occasion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just help us, what are we left with?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We're left with a catastrophic collapse from which she doesn't recover and air in the great vessels on post-mortem.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, there have been two collapses beforehand, haven't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The third event may follow from the first two events, mightn't it, if there's some mechanism at work?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I don't think so.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So what we're actually left with is the rapidity, you say, of a collapse and air in the great vessels?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's not just the rapidity of the collapse, it's the catastrophic nature of the collapse. [Baby D] then had the final episode, which was a complete circulatory collapse, from which she could not be resuscitated. For most pathological disorders in children when they have a collapse, you are able to resuscitate them at least in the short term, even if they don't survive in the long term. It is very unusual for us to have no obvious cause of a collapse and for us not to able to resuscitate a baby.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we want to identify air embolus with any precision, you're relying upon, in fact, what Owen Arthurs says about air in the great vessels, aren't you, and that's it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it wasn't just what Owen Arthurs said, I was given the X-rays, so I could see the air in the great vessels.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But yes, Dr Arthurs has given his evidence this morning.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, he's the expert dealing with paediatric radiology, isn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, he absolutely is.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, and so we have what he says about that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right. The inability to resuscitate you identify as a characteristic of an air embolus, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, we've talked about how it can be fatal in the case of [Baby A]. But you know whatever happened with [Baby D] to cause events 1 and 2 self-evidently wasn't fatal, was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In fact, she made a full and relatively rapid recovery on both occasions?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Which, in principle, is inconsistent with air embolus, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I don't think it is.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree that air embolus in the research and the literature that we have is nearly always fatal?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, what we know is that it depends on the volume and speed of delivery of the gas. So it isn't always fatal at all.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, first of all, in the reported cases do you agree that it is invariably fatal?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it's seen in -- as I've said, most of the literature is based on adults and it's seen in adult practice around particular types of surgery, and it isn't fatal, there is a treatment.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And animals, you've said?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree that animals have got different physiological systems to neonates?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Animals do, but it's clearly not ethical to do some of these studies in humans, so we're left with doing animal studies, and quite often the piglet is used because the physiology of a piglet is very similar to the physiology of a neonate. So some of the studies were in piglets.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm not looking at the question of how difficult it is to do research, I'm looking at the question of how safe it is to rely upon what you say comes from one area and apply it into another. You understand that, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I understand that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. So first of all, a piglet, a rat, a monkey or a dog cannot be said to mirror the conditions of a neonate, can they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Animal models can be made to be very close to -- not a rat. We don't do experiments on monkeys anymore, very rarely, but the piglet model is used quite a lot in neonatal research.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree, whether using a piglet or a dog, you cannot just extrapolate that to the effect on a baby, can you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not directly, but sometimes that's the only method of research that we have.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, a paper you cited, the Gordy paper, refers to rabbits and dogs, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. But you must -- do you not agree, just because something is the case with a rabbit or a dog, it doesn't follow it's going to be the same with a neonate 3 days old, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It may not be, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What basis do you have for saying how much air over what period of time is fatal and how much air over what period of time in a baby weighing 3kg is not fatal?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What basis do you have for that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I've only got the evidence in the literature.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Which is based on dogs and rabbits?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. It's based on dogs and rabbits because it's not ethical to inject humans with air to see who survives and who dies.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That may be the case, but we're looking at the basis for what you're saying, not the difficulties of research.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: My Lord, I'm going to move to an entirely different topic.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, if that's a convenient point to have a break. Could you be ready to continue at 2 o'clock, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 2 o'clock, members of the jury. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
It would be helpful -- I'm not asking for a categoric time -- but about how much longer are we going to be?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think I will be about 35 minutes to 40 minutes, my Lord, not longer than that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's fine.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If we start at 2.00 and my learned friend's estimate is right, we'll definitely be finished by 3.00.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you very much, that's helpful.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The short adjournment)
(In the presence of the jury)
Yes, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Dr Bohin, I'm going to look at [Baby D]'s condition -- not all of it, but aspects of it -- during the 36 hours that she was alive, and I'm going to suggest to you that you have disregarded or minimised certain facts that go to show how unwell she was. Do you agree or disagree with me?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: What, that you're going to show me?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No. Do you agree or disagree that you have sought to minimise certain facts that show how unwell she was?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I have not.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Could we put up, please, slide 118 on the screens? If we go behind that to page 2214.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask some questions about this first -- sorry, in a moment. But I'm going to suggest to you, right really from the moment of birth, there is no doubt that [Baby D] was very unwell; do you agree or disagree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I disagree.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You pointed out that the Apgar scores show 8 at 5 and 9 at 10. They're actually recorded on here but we know that's what they recorded, Dr Bohin. Yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Then we come to a point, 12 minutes later, when we see a description about how [Baby D] presented.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Putting aside whether the Apgar scores are a proper reflection of the moment of birth, I'm going to suggest there is no doubt that by 12 minutes of age she was very unwell indeed; do you agree or disagree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, at 12 minutes of age she had an event, which needed some sort of intervention. As I explained, whether that was an illness or a mechanical obstruction, we can't tell from what is written there.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've heard a lot about the importance of looking at the whole clinical picture with a baby, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Wouldn't you agree that if we look at the whole picture, the clinical picture over [Baby D]'s life, that event at 12 minutes indicates she was very unwell?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it indicates that she had an event which needed some intervention.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You suggested that it may be down to the way in which her father was holding her, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I have suggested that's one possibility, that the way she was held meant that her head flexed on to her chest and obstructed her airway.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I said that was one of the possibilities, I didn't say that was the only possibility.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Not very confident... fathers... new fathers can be very unconfident about holding a baby. The chin can go on to the chest and it can cause a collapse. I can't tell if it's a clinical collapse, meaning through ill health, or a mechanical blockage."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's what you said. When you said mechanical blockage, you meant that's down to the father not holding the baby correctly, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. I'm not -- I've made it very clear that I was not holding [Father of Baby D] responsible for this. I said any new parent is often very nervous about holding their baby and it's very easy, even for nursing staff when they're holding babies, for the baby's chin to fall on to their chest and accidentally compromise the airway. So I was not holding [Father of Baby D] responsible for that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When [Mother of Baby D] gave her evidence she described how when [Baby D] was delivered and lifted over for her to see, the screen, she was asked what the impression was that she had of [Baby D]'s state, and she said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Not alive. She seemed very lifeless. She didn't scream. There was no sound."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just so we can be quite clear, what do you say that may be due to? What are your choices with that, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just been delivered by caesarean section. The cord hadn't even been cut so [Baby D] had just been taken from her mother's abdomen. And the practice of the obstetricians is to hold the baby up to let the parents see the baby very quickly. If a baby is in extremis, the obstetricians wouldn't have done that, the cord would have been cut, and she'd been given to the medical team to intervene to resuscitate her. The fact is she was held up for her mother to see and then they waited 2 minutes before they cut -- clamped and cut the cord.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They wouldn't have done that if the baby was in extremis.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I am going to move on but I am going to suggest to you, in light of the whole clinical picture, that has far more to do with the likelihood of infection than anything about the way her father held her. Do you agree or disagree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm saying you can't tell which of those things it is, whether it is a mechanical obstruction or an illness from infection.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We'll move on and we can see in the note describing:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "In her dad's arms, lost colour, floppy. Five rescue breaths. Two minutes IPDV."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that should be IPPV.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: IPPV:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Then reviewed by the SHO. On arrival, good respiratory effort. Then starting to grunt in theatre.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Reviewed at 1.5 hours by the SHO. Grunting but otherwise obs okay."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And examined normally.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. And then:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Bleeped again as midwife not happy with her colour, lack of response, poor feeding. Brought to unit for screen. On arrival, looked dusky and poor respiratory effort."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If one is to look at the whole of that picture, that's consistent with an infective process, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The grunting and the low temperature, which isn't mentioned there, is consistent with an infective process and by the time she was transferred to the neonatal unit with low saturations and a poor respiratory effort, yes, it was clear there was an infective process going on.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I am suggesting it was obvious right from the outset she was unwell, but you disagree with that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And I suggest to you you are minimising how unwell she was and you disagree with that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not minimising everything -- anything. I'm taking all the evidence put in front of me and making a decision based on that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Before she went to the neonatal unit [Mother of Baby D] gave us some evidence about how [Baby D] presented when she actually had the chance to hold her. I'd like you to help us with whether this is consistent with an infective process rather than anything mechanical. She said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I was really worried because I obviously couldn't move so they brought her to my chest."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is some time after the initial presentation:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "We had skin-to-skin and she didn't really have any movement, she was quite limp. She didn't have a good colour. She looked a bit grey. Then a bit purple. Not really an even colour. She seemed to struggle to breathe. She was making those grunting noises, she wasn't really responsive. There was a split second when she sort of opened her eyes a little bit and looked at me — that's the one picture I've got of her -- and then no response. I tried to breastfeed her and she was completely limp, so yes, I was quite worried."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We can see on the notes where there's reference to "no feeding". That's a very poorly baby, isn't it, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's the interpretation of a very worried mother. But I can't think that the midwifery staff would be allowing a baby who was limp with a poor colour to remain on the post-natal ward. I don't know what time -- how old [Baby D] was when [Mother of Baby D] made those comments, but she was poorly by the time she went to the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: [Mother of Baby D] was clearly worried about her daughter and she may have been poorly at that time, but I can't think that the midwifery staff would allow her to feed or attempt to feed and stay on a post-natal ward if they were concerned about her clinical condition.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They, the staff, or one or more members of staff looking after her before she went to the neonatal unit failed to ensure that she was received antibiotics at the appropriate time, didn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It wouldn't have been the midwifery staff's role to give her antibiotics at any time. It was the medical staff that would have been giving antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And there was a failure to give them, wasn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They failed to give them in a timely way, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's the day she was born. I'm not going to go through all of that; you've been asked about it this morning.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We know that she was ventilated overnight. Do you agree that's consistent with a child that's suffering from infection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's consistent with, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You told the jury that when we get to 21 June, [Baby D], you said, remained well all day. Do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've heard that that morning, when she was taken off the ventilator, her blood gases deteriorated and we've seen the chart, dropping below the appropriate level.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you not agree that's an indication of being in less than optimal health?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She was taken off the ventilator and didn't initially manage and therefore the medical staff intervened and gave her the support that she needed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And a healthy child would manage off a ventilator, wouldn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, not always.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So you don't regard the fact that her blood gases deteriorated when she came off the ventilator as a sign of bad health?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, that wasn't the question you previously asked me.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, the poor blood gases is a sign that something may be amiss. The fact that she didn't manage off the ventilator isn't necessarily a sign of poor health, which is what you asked me in the previous question.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right. Do you agree the low blood gases are a sign of bad health?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They can be. But a single blood gas would not be interpreted in isolation, so you would look at a trend and you would put it in the clinical context of what else was happening with the baby at the time.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Up until 12 o'clock the blood gases remained low, didn't they? That was a trend?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You'd have to show the blood gases because I can't --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can we put up slide 12, please. You can go behind that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We can look at the top half, please. Scroll down a little bit more actually. Thank you. We can see these. Can you cease these clearly, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I can see them.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we look at 10.14, which is after she'd been taken off the ventilator and just before she had to go on to the CPAP, her blood gases show acidosis, don't they (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, they do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: 12.10, even though she's been on put CPAP, the blood gas has worsened slightly, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A little bit.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. So up to that point there's a movement of travel that is not so good; would you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'd say the blood gases have deteriorated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right, deteriorated. That's not the same as remaining well all day, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, she came off the ventilator because that was the right thing to do. She didn't manage, was started on respiratory support. It took a while to settle, so we've got a 10.14 gas, which is sub-optimal, and so she started CPAP. Two hours after that the blood gas had not improved, but 2 hours after that it had and was normal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, it did. And an unwell baby can have periods of improving and deteriorating, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not quite like that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: A baby can improve, don't you agree, and then deteriorate?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, they can improve and slowly deteriorate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They could deteriorate rapidly, couldn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You'd have other signs -- you wouldn't just go on a blood gas, you'd have other signs. You'd look at the other clinical parameters.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Like if they had pneumonia in their lungs or something like that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, you'd look at the other clinical parameters. We know that [Baby D]'s got pneumonia in her lungs through all of these blood gases.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Does that influence at all your view on whether she is well all day, that she had pneumonia?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, because she did have pneumonia, there's no doubt about that, and I was very clear about that this morning, she does have pneumonia. But she had responded to antibiotics and was improving and she managed off the ventilator for a short time and then was coping on CPAP.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She didn't need to go back on the ventilator so actually her other parameters had improved.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree that she didn't cope very well off CPAP that day --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She didn't --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- later on?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Later on that day?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Let me remind you. We can go to the slide if you want but we've seen reference in the clinical notes and in the nursing notes that at about 7.15, when she was given period off the CPAP, she desaturated, didn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, and was out back on very quickly. There wasn't a blood gas in between, I don't think.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No, but however quickly she was put back on, the fact that a baby desaturates without breathing assistance like that is a sign of or a potential sign of poor health, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, not necessarily. You have to take everything into context. It was reasonable to try her off CPAP and you can't keep babies on CPAP forever so it's reasonable to try them off when you think they are stable enough to try off. So the clinical team made what I think was a good judgement call to try her off CPAP. She didn't manage, the CPAP is immediately available to put back on and things are safe.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So she wasn't stable enough to stay off CPAP then, was she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No. And that is not a sign of being well all day, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's not a sign of a deteriorating baby, it's a sign of a baby who needs a small bit of respiratory support, who is in air, whose saturations are normal, but is otherwise stable. She couldn't manage off CPAP, it's perfectly acceptable while she is being treated for her pneumonia to CPAP until such time as she didn't need it any longer.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You told the jury that between 23.52 and 01.14 that morning her blood gases were satisfactory; do you remember saying that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And in fact, in your report which you were referred to, paragraph 5.17, you said that she had normal blood gases. You say at 5.17:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Although [Baby D] had pneumonia, she was clinically well, was in air and had normal blood gases."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you see that? Now, you have just said then about it's okay for her to be on CPAP, she's all right if she's not deteriorating. With all of that in mind let's look at what happens after 18.44. So let's scroll down, please, and see what follows.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we look at 2352, as against 18.44, that is a deterioration isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a change. I personally wouldn't be worried about that because she's remained in air.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: First of all, is it a deterioration in terms of blood gas?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, not necessarily. You have to take it in the round.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If I saw that blood gas, I wouldn't be particularly concerned about it.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is it an improvement in blood gas?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is it the same as the one before?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What is it then by reference to the one before?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's different.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's different. Not as good, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's not as good but it's marginal so it isn't a concern, it wouldn't be a concern to me.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's not normal, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But neither is it very abnormal and in the clinical context it wouldn't be a concern to me.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We know the various clinical features, I'm not going to list them all. We see at 01.14 a blood gas. And what's the direction of travel in terms of blood gas between 23.52 and 01.14?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's more of a metabolic component in that blood gas, in that the pH has drifted down very slightly, but the base excess has gone -- increased to minus 8.9. So there's now much more of a metabolic component rather than a respiratory component.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That doesn't make it better, does it? Metabolic acidosis is still a problem, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't say they were better. I said they were no different. I didn't say it was better, I didn't say it had improved.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You said there is now a base excess of minus 8.9. Is that better 0or worse than a base excess of minus 5.6?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's worse than a base excess of minus 5.6.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Are you sure you're not trying to minimise in any way how poorly [Baby D] was?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not trying to minimise anything and I would like to make it clear my duty is to the court, to look at all the evidence, in an impartial way, that's put before me and I think that is what I have done.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, when you say these blood gas readings at 23.52 and 01.14 are normal in your report, they are not normal blood gas readings, are they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They are not a concern to me. If I'd seen those blood gases in the clinical context of [Baby D] at that time I would not be concerned.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The detail -- the detail of the neonatal condition and readings relating to it can provide early warning signals, can't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the point of having a unit with specialists who can see the detail is to look out for, for example, signals like that, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, signals -- like what?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Looking out for details.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The whole point of having a unit with specialists to look at the details is to pick up the subtle signs that may indicate the direction of travel for a little baby, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And if practitioners choose to disregard details, there's not much point in the unit monitoring them at all, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think you need to look at people's expertise and background and their experience in looking after sick children and making decisions based not out of a textbook but from their clinical experience and looking at the infant's clinical condition in the round.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And in my experience, if I'd seen those blood gases, I would note the trend but I wouldn't be particularly worried about them. Somebody else may see them and may have a different view. My view, which is what I'm being asked to give in the court, is that I wouldn't be concerned about them. I would note the trend and, if the trend continued, I would intervene.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What's the point of having these details at all then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: To look for trends and put it into a clinical context so that you can intervene if necessary.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And we see, do we, at 23.52 and 01.14, certainly within the parameters we have, a deterioration in that trend don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think that there's a deterioration. I think I've probably already said that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Dr Evans in his reports didn't actually refer to these two readings, though he did, he didn't refer to these ones at all, he didn't include the ones that you call normal. Did you notice that about his reports when you did yours?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Are you scrutinising Dr Evans closely, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but there are lots of other things that he didn't write down, I assume. But no, I... I didn't scrutinise every single reading, every single observation for every single baby in his reports.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At the same time as we have this blood gas reading, we also have low sodium levels, don't we, with [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, they're marginally low.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They may be a little bit low but isn't some of the skill of neonatal medicine to be able top look at small details?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And we know, do you agree, keep this in mind, she had pneumonia at this time, didn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And do you agree or disagree that she had been very well -- very unwell within a 12-hour period before this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I don't think she was very unwell. I think she had a pneumonia, it required respiratory support, and she was responding appropriately to that respiratory support and to the antibiotics that she had been given.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So when you say she had been well all day, does that take into account how she performed when taken off CPAP?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can I be clear about that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But I think that's just a minor blip in clinical care.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Looking at the overall picture, she had not had any major deteriorations throughout the day and so that was why I made that comment.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, I suggest to you that when you put together what she had in terms of her history to this point and what we see on the blood gas and the sodium, she couldn't possibly be described as "well all day". Do you agree or disagree with me?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I disagree with you.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we just consider the events at 01.30 and 3 am. Both of them could be regarded as warning signs that [Baby D] was unwell, couldn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They could.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As to the decision, let me ask you this, to take her off CPAP after the second one of those events, you heard the evidence of Dr Newby, didn't you, when she talked about that decision?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you hear that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She could come off in that situation -- in fact, it was before the second event. She said that after the first event, there would be a low threshold to intervene by way of ventilation if there were further desaturations.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. So after the first event, Dr Newby had said there was a low threshold to intervene. There then was another desaturation, wasn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And if one were to follow through the logic of what Dr Newby said about a low threshold to intervene, that would have been a proper time to increase the type of ventilation, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily because (a) Dr Newby wasn't there at the time, Dr Brunton was the clinician who was faced with [Baby D]. He had been told by the nursing staff that she had been distressed and so by the time he got there, she had recovered from her desaturation and, because of the story given to him about being distressed, he felt it prudent, rather than take the step to give medication to paralyse her and put her back on the ventilator, he was faced with a baby who was then -- by then in air and saturating normally and felt the right decision was to
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: try her off CPAP, knowing that if that hadn't worked he could put her back on. And I think that was a reasonable decision to make.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When you said earlier to the jury his decision that she could be fed with breast milk shows how stable she was because Dr Brunton wouldn't have decided to do that if she was unstable, one alternative is that was simply a bad decision, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's not a bad decision if you look at the clinical parameters at the time because there was no clinical reason not to feed her. Everything else was stable in terms of heart rate, respiratory rate, saturations, she was in air. All of that was stable so there was no clinical reason not to feed her. So you know, in defence of him, I don't think that was a bad decision.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm not talking about the decision to feed. What I am saying is when you say that he felt she could be fed and that goes to show she must have been stable, it may just be that taking her off CPAP was a bad decision, not that he then could feed her so she must have been stable.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think taking her off CPAP was a reasonable decision to make given the clinical parameters he was faced with.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There is nothing that we have seen for the time he took her off CPAP to suggest that, in terms of respiration, she would perform better off it than on it, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The collapse that happens at 3.45 could be explained as consistent with a worsening physical condition because of an infective process, couldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, because -- no, I don't agree with that at all. She remained in air -- if she had a deteriorating pneumonia or other condition you would expect her not to be in air, to have increased oxygen requirement, you would expect her respiratory rate to have gone up, and you would have expected her to be desaturating and she wasn't doing any of those things immediately prior to that final collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, I suggest to you, we know she was born with pneumonia; do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We know that certainly throughout her very short life she was ill at times with respiratory illness. Do you agree with that? Respiratory infection.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She had a respiratory infection, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree it made her ill at various points?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She required a brief period of ventilation early on, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree she had respiratory difficulties throughout her life?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree she couldn't actually breathe for any period of time without getting some sort of assistance?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She couldn't though, Dr Bohin. She's on CPAP nearly the whole time.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She was taken off the ventilator and managed for an hour and a half before she went back on CPAP.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And she's put back on CPAP because her blood gases deteriorated, didn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And then she was stable on CPAP.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, and my question was: do you agree that she couldn't manage breathing properly without the assistance of CPAP?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At that time, yes, because she was still recovering from her pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as we know she couldn't cope with coming off CPAP at least up until the point that she was taken off after event 2, could she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, I'm not -- I don't understand the question. She was on respiratory support, so we wouldn't have known whether she could manage or not unless we took her off to see.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And do you agree that when she died, I don't think there's any dispute on this, the post-mortem identified pneumonia in her lungs and acute lung damage?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was the interpretation of the initial pathologist, yes, that the right lung showed pneumonia, the right lung more than the left lung, but there was evidence of pneumonia in both lungs with hyaline membranes, which is an indication of acute lung injury.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So if we put the whole clinical picture together, as we are encouraged to do, all of that makes it entirely possible that infection could have been causative in death, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I think [Baby D] died with pneumonia not because of her pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you have minimised the clinical factors showing how bad the infection was, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I have not done that. I have looked at all the evidence in the round, which is what I'm supposed to do as an expert witness.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What you have done is to be, with regard to [Baby D], influenced by the allegation you're looking at rather than the underlying medical facts; that's what's happened, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Does your Lordship have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, that's it at this stage, Dr Bohin.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. You know you'll be coming back again. What I said before obviously still applies.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
Right, Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I have two things to do, my Lord. One is to recall Kate Tyndall to deal with one or two corrections to the sequence, which will take 5 or 10 minutes, and then (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Fine. So we'll carry on, obviously, we've only been going half an hour.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: These corrections, you're going to put them in evidence, what they are?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, I'm going to adduce the evidence of the corrections and they'll be automatically updated on the system. There is a piece of paper just to prove how old-fashioned I am as well.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MRS KATE TYNDALL (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Welcome back, Mrs Tyndall. Would you just identify yourself for the sake of the recording, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm Kate Tyndall, intelligence analyst.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you very much. I think you have a few corrections to make as to the sequence of events, first of all, and then you have a piece of paper which has a diagram on it to help the jury as well. Is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. If Mr Murphy could help, do we start with slide 143?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
